title: The Quantum Atom: Orbitals and the Pauli Principle

cards.h: Why the periodic table has its shape
cards.b: Chemistry is the study of how atoms hold together, and it is all about electrons. Why do sodium and potassium behave alike, and neon and argon never react? Quantum theory answers: electrons live in orbitals, and a rule from Wolfgang Pauli (1925) forbids two of them from sharing the same state.

Schrödinger's equation gives the electron in hydrogen a set of allowed standing waves. Each is an orbital: a cloud-shaped region showing where the electron is likely to be found (the size squared of its wavefunction). The ground state, "1s", is a sphere. Next come a sphere (2s) and three dumbbell shapes (2p), then five clover shapes (3d), and so on.

The cloud is an odds map, not a path. Many electron "orbits" are replaced by "regions of likely find".

An electron state needs four labels: n (shell, sets size and energy), l (shape: s, p, d, f), m (orientation) and spin (up or down). Their allowed values follow from fitting waves, as in the guitar string picture. In an atom, each shell n has n² orbitals, so 2n² places for electrons: 2, 8, 18, 32.

cards.h: No two in the same state
cards.b: Electrons are fermions: no two can share all four labels. So each orbital holds at most two electrons, one spin up and one spin down. Pauli proposed this in 1925 to explain the structure of the table and anomalous spectra; he won the 1945 Nobel Prize.

Fill orbitals from lowest energy upward and you get the periodic table: row lengths 2, 8, 8, 18... Elements in one column share the number of electrons in their outer shell, so behave alike: lithium, sodium and potassium each have a single outer electron to give away. Noble gases have full outer shells and do not react. Bonds form when atoms share or swap electrons to fill shells.

Imagine a hotel in which rooms come in set sizes and each room holds at most two guests of opposite habit. New guests take the cheapest free room. The outermost floor is what guests see, and it decides how they mix with other hotels.

Where it breaks: electrons are identical and have no names. You cannot say which electron is in which room.

Pauli exclusion keeps atoms from squashing together and gives matter its volume. In 1967 Freeman Dyson and Andrew Lenard proved that without it, ordinary matter would collapse to a tiny fraction of its size, and its size would not even scale with the amount of stuff. Your solidity is quantum.

Atomic spectra show lines matching the predicted levels, with extra splitting from spin. Ionisation energies jump after a shell is emptied: a clear fingerprint of shells. In 2000s experiments, electron clouds of single atoms have been imaged directly, for example hydrogen orbitals using photoionisation microscopy (Stodolna et al., 2013).

• "Electrons orbit like planets." They form probability clouds.
  • "Pauli is a force." It is a rule from the symmetry of identical fermions, not a push.
  • "Orbitals are fixed solid shapes." They are odds maps that change when atoms bond.

Meghnad Saha's 1920 ionisation equation used atomic energy levels to read stellar spectra. C.V. Raman and K.S. Krishnan's spectroscopy (1928) probes molecular energy levels. Indian quantum chemists such as Charusita Chakravarty and others work on computing orbitals for materials; the National Quantum Mission funds quantum materials work at IIT Delhi.

• Orbitals are odds clouds with four labels (n, l, m, spin).
  • Pauli (1925): no two electrons share the same state; each orbital holds two.
  • Shell filling explains the periodic table and keeps matter from collapsing.

Think about it

  1. Why are sodium and potassium chemically alike?
  2. What would the periodic table look like without the Pauli principle?
